canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats natural language understanding as a broad model capacity to comprehend and interpret human language, text, or instructions across tasks. Many definitions frame it as a latent or general ability, covering meaning, intent, context, nuance, and semantic content, and some extend it to prompts, task descriptions, natural-language queries, or open-ended commands that must be turned into internal or formal representations. A smaller line of work treats it behaviorally, as performance on task families such as classification, inference, similarity, paraphrase, acceptability judgment, or multilingual question answering. The main difference across definitions is whether the construct is presented as an internal capacity or as observable task performance, and whether it stays broad or is narrowed to settings such as retrieval verification, crossword clues, formal language conversion, or embodied instructions.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for overlapping ideas, including language understanding, language comprehension, linguistic understanding, text understanding, text comprehension, natural language comprehension, input comprehension, general language understanding, and text-level understanding. The most common organization is task-based: classification, natural language inference or textual entailment, similarity or paraphrase, acceptability, and question answering recur as representative facets, while some papers isolate narrower facets such as contextual word meaning, entity tracking as a facet of language comprehension, or instruction-following across linguistic variations. One recurring usage treats natural language inference as a popular way of evaluating natural language understanding, whereas other papers discuss it alongside reasoning, generation, world knowledge, or embodied reasoning rather than using one label for all of them.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is dominated by benchmark evaluation. Papers link the construct to 29 measurement instruments and 6 behavioral indicators, with GLUE most often, followed by ARC-Challenge, CoLA, MMLU, and ARC-Easy. These measures are mostly benchmark suites or datasets: GLUE is repeatedly used as a collection of sentence classification, similarity, paraphrase, and inference tasks, while other instruments are described as multiple-choice or task suites assessing various aspects of natural language understanding. The linked behavioral indicators extend the construct into inference, puzzle-like comprehension, chronological ordering, and text-based action settings, so the operationalization mostly matches the broad task-centered definitions, though some measures move into reasoning-heavy, multilingual, or embodied settings.

Links. Links beyond measurement are sparse. One paper claims a causal relationship from Memorization to natural language understanding, and other papers claim causal relationships from natural language understanding to Planning and to Text generation. Separate papers report that it is related to Contextual reasoning and to application tasks such as Text-to-SQL and knowledge graph question answering, both described as requiring natural language understanding. No correlational links are reported.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the prevailing usage treats natural language understanding as a broad model capacity to comprehend and interpret human language, text, or instructions across tasks. Many definitions frame it as a latent or general ability, covering meaning, intent, context, nuance, and semantic content, and some extend it to prompts, task descriptions, natural-language queries, or open-ended commands that must be turned into internal or formal representations. A smaller line of work treats it behaviorally, as performance on task families such as classification, inference, similarity, paraphrase, acceptability judgment, or multilingual question answering. The main difference across definitions is whether the construct is presented as an internal capacity or as observable task performance, and whether it stays broad or is narrowed to settings such as retrieval verification, crossword clues, formal language conversion, or embodied instructions.

characterization_sections.label: Space of facets.
characterization_sections.text: Papers use several near-synonymous labels for overlapping ideas, including language understanding, language comprehension, linguistic understanding, text understanding, text comprehension, natural language comprehension, input comprehension, general language understanding, and text-level understanding. The most common organization is task-based: classification, natural language inference or textual entailment, similarity or paraphrase, acceptability, and question answering recur as representative facets, while some papers isolate narrower facets such as contextual word meaning, entity tracking as a facet of language comprehension, or instruction-following across linguistic variations. One recurring usage treats natural language inference as a popular way of evaluating natural language understanding, whereas other papers discuss it alongside reasoning, generation, world knowledge, or embodied reasoning rather than using one label for all of them.

characterization_sections.label: Space of measurement.
characterization_sections.text: Operationalization is dominated by benchmark evaluation. Papers link the construct to 29 measurement instruments and 6 behavioral indicators, with GLUE most often, followed by ARC-Challenge, CoLA, MMLU, and ARC-Easy. These measures are mostly benchmark suites or datasets: GLUE is repeatedly used as a collection of sentence classification, similarity, paraphrase, and inference tasks, while other instruments are described as multiple-choice or task suites assessing various aspects of natural language understanding. The linked behavioral indicators extend the construct into inference, puzzle-like comprehension, chronological ordering, and text-based action settings, so the operationalization mostly matches the broad task-centered definitions, though some measures move into reasoning-heavy, multilingual, or embodied settings.

characterization_sections.label: Links.
characterization_sections.text: Links beyond measurement are sparse. One paper claims a causal relationship from Memorization to natural language understanding, and other papers claim causal relationships from natural language understanding to Planning and to Text generation. Separate papers report that it is related to Contextual reasoning and to application tasks such as Text-to-SQL and knowledge graph question answering, both described as requiring natural language understanding. No correlational links are reported.
